first-semester.title: Fall 2025
first-semester.intro: My first semester as an undergraduate teaching assistant for Writing for the Health Professions. These artifacts connect classroom discussion, accessible health communication, and my developing approach to feedback.

entries.title: Creating inclusive classrooms
entries.body:
One of Chickering and Gamson’s Seven Principles that I connect with the most is the idea of student–faculty contact. While I also agree with Ellie, Daria, and Natalie that prompt feedback is essential, I think contact goes a step further because it builds the foundation for feedback to even matter. When I have had professors who were approachable and consistent in their communication, I found myself more motivated to keep up with the work and less anxious about making mistakes. As a UTA, I want to mirror that by being present, whether that is through quick email replies, check-ins before or after class, or just making it clear that students are not bothering me when they reach out. Like Daria mentioned, respecting different ways of learning is also critical. If students feel comfortable approaching me, I will be better positioned to adapt explanations to what works for them.

From Saunders and Kardia’s piece, one assumption that stood out to me was that students from certain backgrounds will naturally know how to navigate college culture. I had not realized how many small things, like understanding office hours, writing emails to professors, or even knowing how grading works in U.S. classrooms, can create barriers for first-generation or international students. Reading this made me think back to when I started college and hesitated to go to office hours simply because I did not know what to expect. Ellie’s point about built-in check-ins resonated with me here; creating structured opportunities for students to talk one-on-one lowers that initial barrier.

Finally, in the “Planning Considerations” section, I appreciated the reminder that instructors will not always have the answers when it comes to cultural or religious practices, but it is our responsibility to learn and adjust. Like Natalie said, making the effort to educate ourselves goes a long way in creating a classroom that feels fair and respectful.
entries.reflection: Reading this again, I still agree that being approachable is one of the most important parts of being a UTA. I know from being a student that it is much easier to ask for help when you feel like the person actually wants to hear from you. What stood out to me more this time was the part about knowing how college works. Things like office hours can seem obvious now, but I remember not really knowing what to expect either. I chose this post because it reminds me to be careful about assuming students already know what to do. My learning log later in the semester mentions students coming up to me for clarification, which was reassuring. I felt like I was starting to become the kind of UTA I had hoped to be.

entries.title: Responding to student writing
entries.body:
My biggest takeaway from this week is that feedback should feel like a real conversation with the student, not just a list of what they did right or wrong. The point of responding to writing is to teach the writer something about their process, not just grade the paper. When feedback feels thoughtful and personal, students are more likely to take it seriously and use it to improve.

What stood out to me in Responding to Student Writing was the idea of writing final comments like a short letter to the student. It makes the feedback feel more personal and supportive. Starting with something like “Dear [student’s name]” helps remind me that I’m talking to a person, not just responding to a document. I also liked how the reading suggested restating the paper’s main idea before moving into praise and critique. That shows the student you really read and understood what they were trying to say. In the essay on Barbara Ehrenreich, for example, I might start by noting that the student clearly understands Ehrenreich’s main message about the cycle of poverty and then give feedback on how to make the argument flow more smoothly. This approach gives the student confidence in what they did well while showing them what they can work on next.

If I applied this to my own feedback, I would try to make sure my comments sound like I’m rooting for the student to grow as a writer, not just pointing out flaws.

Discussion question:
What are some ways we can make our written comments sound more like a conversation and less like a critique?
entries.reflection: This was one of my favorite discussions because giving feedback was probably the responsibility I worried about most. I wanted to be helpful, but I also understood how discouraging comments can feel when you have worked hard on something. I still really like the idea of writing comments as a short letter. It is a simple change, but it reminds me that there is a person reading what I write. Looking back, I think the challenge is making feedback both encouraging and useful. Being nice does not help much if the student still has no idea what to change! I chose this post because it shows me working through that balance. My final essay comes back to the same topic, especially how much feedback can matter when students still have time to revise.

entries.title: Finding my voice as a UTA
entries.body:
After two months, I have definitely acclimatized to being a UTA and am glad to say that many of my concerns ended up working themselves out. I was extremely worried about leaving students effective feedback on assignments and did not want to be condescending while also being helpful. While it has been a learning process, I feel I have grown a lot as a UTA, not only in giving effective feedback, but also in terms of comfort overall. Students often come up to me asking for clarification, which makes me feel like, at the very least, I am approachable.

I have grown quite close to my professor, and I feel quite comfortable asking them for advice, and they even ask me for advice too! I was really worried about overstepping as a UTA, but my professor allows me to have a voice in the classroom, which I really appreciate. I also feel like I know my peer UTAs much better, especially thanks to the weekly student-led discussions; I am a big fan of them.

Overall, I really enjoy TAing for my professional writing class, and hope to participate in the coming semesters as I am able to.
entries.reflection: It is nice to read this again because I remember how worried I was at the beginning of that semester. I was comfortable talking to people, but being someone students came to for academic advice felt different. By this point, I felt much more comfortable with both the students and my professor. The part about my professor asking for my advice still stands out to me. I had been so concerned about overstepping that having my perspective welcomed meant a lot. Looking back, I think that support was a big reason I became more confident. I also meant what I said about enjoying the student-led discussions. Hearing other UTAs talk through the same concerns was reassuring, and it made me realize that we were all learning how to do this as we went.

entries.title: AI in the context of writing
entries.description: Group presentation · Fall 2025 · With Emily Charron, Alexander Green, and Natalie Ventura-Diaz
entries.reflection: This was a rather fun presentation to put together, especially because everyone already had something to say about AI. Our group divided the work pretty evenly, and we tried to make the class participate from the beginning instead of just listening to us talk. The tone activity and guessing game gave people something to react to, which helped move us into the harder questions about writing and independent thinking. My part included discussing possible signs of AI use and bringing classmates’ discussion responses into the conversation. Looking back, I think the uncertainty was one of the most useful parts. We could talk about patterns, but that did not mean we could know for sure how something was written. I still think explaining why the writing process matters is more useful than simply telling students not to use AI.
entries.supportingText:
ENGL388V Group Lesson 
Emily Charron,  Alexander Green, Nathaniel Monteparte, Natalie Ventura-Diaz
Readings
* Instructions 
   * Go through the required reading and then read at least one of the additional readings. Do not spend too much time reading them entirely, but rather try to find the author's key arguments for or against AI usage. Take mental notes to help you formulate your responses to the discussion questions. 


Reading 1 (Required, Scholarly):
* Are we witnessing the Death of the Writer?
* From module
* Horton, Randall. “Are We Witnessing the Death of the Writer? Facing the AI Crossroads in Class and on the Page.” Salon, 23 Sept. 2023, www.salon.com/2023/09/23/are-we-witnessing-the-of-the-writer-facing-the-ai-crossroads-in-class-and-on-the-page/
Reading 2:
* Using AI ethically 
* From module
* The University of Kansas. “Ethical Use of AI in Writing Assignments.” Cte.ku.edu, The University of Kansas, July 2024, cte.ku.edu/ethical-use-ai-writing-assignments. Accessed 15 Oct. 2025.
Reading 3 (Scholarly Source, Not listed in modules):
* Using AI in academic writing: what’s allowed and what’s not
* Scholarly source from elsewhere 
* Laher S. Using AI in academic writing: what’s allowed and what’s not. South African Journal of Psychology. 2025;55(2):155-158. doi:10.1177/00812463251338244
Discussion Questions
1. What do you think of AI? Is it doing more harm or good in writing classes?
2. The first reading makes specific claims about the “Death” of the writer. Do you agree with the author's claims here? Disagree?
3. What is your instructor's policy on AI? Is it effective? Do you agree with it?
4. As a UTA, have you experienced any situations where you suspected AI usage in assignments? If so, how did you handle it with your instructor? If not, how would you handle it?
Please answer the questions that stand out to you the most in 250-300 words, do not try to answer all of them. Then, please respond to at least 1 peer in roughly 150 words.

entries.title: Making health information accessible
entries.description: Revised lesson plan · Canva, plain language, and audience-centered infographics · November 2025
entries.reflection: My peers were definitely right that the original version needed more time. I had planned a demonstration, a plain-language lesson, group work, presentations, and an exit ticket in 45 minutes, which was probably a bit ambitious! Expanding it to 60 minutes gave the group activity and presentations more room. The feedback also helped me clarify how students would receive comments on their work. I chose this lesson because it connects directly to why I enjoy Writing for the Health Professions: knowing the science is important, but being able to explain it to someone else matters too. I like that students would actually make something instead of just hearing about good design. At the time I wrote the revision, I had not taught the lesson yet, so my reflection here is on the planning and peer feedback.

entries.title: First-semester final synthesis essay
entries.description: December 2025 · Feedback, belonging, and independent thinking
entries.body:
When I stepped into the role of a UTA for professional writing, my comfort level in certain areas of teaching was rather skewed. Socially, I have always been comfortable connecting with people, and public speaking has never been something that intimidated me. Leadership positions in a variety of clubs on campus, as well as president of the wrestling team, instilled natural and effective communication. Translating to UTA work, I knew how to read a room, jump into conversations, and help students feel at ease during class discussions. What genuinely scared me was the other responsibilities that came with the role. For the first time, my words had real academic consequences. One of my biggest concerns early on was responding to student writing. Giving feedback felt “heavy”. I knew that what I wrote could shape how students revised, how they understood the assignment, and even how they viewed themselves as writers. That last point holds a great amount of weight because only a semester ago I was in their shoes, and I understand the feeling when you work hard on an assignment and receive feedback crtizing your work. In some cases, my comments also factored into grades, which made the pressure feel even greater. At the same time, I wanted to make sure I was fully aligned with my professor’s expectations and the course rubric. Balancing my own instincts with those standards was a challenge I had not anticipated.
The Princeton Writing Program’s piece on responding to student writing helped me rethink what feedback is supposed to do. Instead of treating comments as corrections or justifications for a grade, the reading frames feedback as a conversation between the reader and writer. That shift mattered a lot for me. It helped me move away from the urge to comment on everything and toward focusing on patterns, asking questions, and giving students a few clear, meaningful areas to work on. Once I let go of the idea that good feedback meant saying everything, the process felt more manageable and more purposeful. One experience that really stayed with me involved commenting on a student’s draft for a rather large assignment. After receiving my feedback, the student told me that because it was given at the draft stage, it allowed them to rethink their approach entirely and revise in a way that actually made sense to them. While the assignment was still graded and held to the rubric, that moment felt bigger than grading. It felt like I had played a role in how the student learned to think through their writing, not just how they fixed it. That experience made the ideas from the Princeton reading feel real rather than theoretical. I feel like not only UTAs but even professors often forget the impact their guidance can have on students. That special relationship between “teacher” and “student” is definitely something I have grown to value, being on both sides of the coin. 
Creating an inclusive classroom environment felt more natural to me, but the readings helped me understand why those efforts mattered. Shari Saunders and Diana Kardia’s work on inclusive classrooms emphasizes that learning is deeply tied to how supported and respected students feel. Inclusivity is not just about who is in the room. It is about how students interact with one another and whether they feel comfortable participating without fear of judgment. I saw this clearly with a student who struggled during the first half of the semester due to an overwhelming workload outside of class (they were also a pre-med student). At first, they seemed disengaged and hesitant to participate, often preoccupied with other work. Over time, as they began talking more with classmates nearby and felt more comfortable contributing, their engagement changed noticeably. As their comfort increased, their performance improved as well. Their grades began to exceed where they had started, which reinforced something I came to believe strongly over the semester: students perform better when they feel comfortable in their environment. That sense of belonging is not a “bonus”. I believe it is foundational to learning. This is also a realization that expanded through many meetings with my professor. Often, we would discuss students who were struggling, and the conversation always started with “how can we help them in their situation?” We both tried to realize that there could very well and often was, another factor in their lives. Overcoming that fundamental attribution error (attributing actions to one’s personality rather than external factors) is something that I think extends beyond teaching. It is something that should be practiced in multiple facets of life. 
The unit on artificial intelligence was one of the most complicated parts of the semester, especially in a professional writing class. AI has changed rapidly even since the beginning of my college experience, and its presence in writing classrooms raises real concerns. In his essay “Are We Witnessing the Death of the Writer?”, Randall Horton argues that the danger of AI is not just plagiarism, but the loss of independent thinking and engagement with the writing process itself. That idea resonated with what I was seeing as a UTA as well as fellow UTAs, considering our in-class presentation ran right to the bell. Rather than approaching AI from a purely punitive standpoint, the course emphasized designing assignments and grading structures that value process and effort. I found that establishing credibility and trust in the classroom mattered more than strict enforcement. This intuitively makes sense because I do believe telling students simply not to use AI will make them want to use it more rather then telling them ‘why’ they should not be using it. When students feel respected and supported, they are more likely to be honest about their work (at least I hope they were). I also truly think the labor-based grading framework reduced stress around grades and shifted the focus toward learning, revision, and participation (I know you as well, believe in this, Professor Forrester). Seeing how effective this was made me wish more fields could adopt similar approaches, even though I recognize the challenges of doing so.
Being a UTA taught me a lot about teaching, but it also taught me how to be a better student. Watching what actually helped students learn, such as peer revision, thoughtful feedback, inclusive environments, and lower grade anxiety, gave me insight into how learning really works. This experience reshaped how I think about education, mentorship, and leadership, and it reminded me that students learn best when they are trusted, supported, and encouraged to use their own thinking. Unfortunately and fortunately, I am studying abroad next semester, preventing me from continuing as a UTA, but I hope to participate in some capacity my senior year because I got so much out of the experience. Even apart from UTA, the ENGL388v discussion was just as valuable. Truth be told, many times I was very stressed from my high workload, and the class was long, but the discussions and insights were very valuable! Everyone in the discussion was extremely nice, and it was reassuring to know we were all going through the same new experiences. Finally, I would like to thank you, Professor, for an amazing year. I know I have had a few not-so-enjoyable life events and also a workload at the end of the semester, but the accommodation is not something that many instructors do, and the understanding means more than you know. I have never been to one of your classes, but I can tell you have the innate ability to put yourself in someone else's shoes. That skill can not be taught, and it is a gift. Good luck next semester with all of your endeavors!
entries.reflection: I chose this essay because it brings together the parts of my first semester that meant the most to me. Reading it again, I can see how much of my experience came back to feedback and relationships with students. I started the semester worried about whether my comments would be useful, and by the end I had a much better understanding of why that responsibility mattered. The moment when a student told me my draft feedback helped them rethink their approach is still one of my favorite examples in the essay. I also still agree with the point about considering what might be going on outside of class before assuming a student does not care. Being a UTA gave me a different perspective on teaching, but it also made me think more carefully about how I learn and respond to guidance myself.

homeIntro: I am Nathaniel Monteparte, a biology major at the University of Maryland and an undergraduate teaching assistant for Writing for the Health Professions. I first took the class as a student, so it has been interesting to come back and see it from the teaching side. This portfolio includes my work from Fall 2025 and Fall 2026, along with reflections on giving feedback, working with students, and helping people understand health information.

lessonSections.heading: Purpose
lessonSections.text: This lesson helps students rewrite complex medical information in plain language and use Canva to create a clear health infographic for a general audience.

lessonSections.heading: Learning objectives
items: Identify features of an effective health infographic.
Rewrite medical or scientific language for a general audience while preserving accuracy.
Use Canva, with optional AI features, to communicate health information visually.
Explain how language and design choices affect accessibility, comprehension, and credibility.

lessonSections.heading: Materials
items: Student devices and Canva access; projector for the demonstration.
Examples of clear and confusing infographics.
A dense but manageable medical paragraph selected from CDC, NIH, or WHO materials.
NIH Plain Language Checklist; warm-up and exit-ticket forms.

lessonSections.heading: 60-minute sequence
table: Identify what makes an infographic effective or confusing.
Model templates, Magic Design, visual hierarchy, contrast, and alternative text.
Compare jargon with everyday wording and introduce the NIH checklist.
Groups of 3–4 simplify a medical paragraph and build an infographic. Circulate to support clarity and accessibility.
Invite 1–2-minute presentations; provide brief feedback on clarity, design, and audience needs. Adjust the number of presentations to class size.
Record three things learned, two design takeaways, and one remaining question.

lessonSections.heading: Evidence of learning
lessonSections.text: Review each group’s infographic and explanation for plain language, factual accuracy, audience fit, visual hierarchy, and accessibility. Use the exit ticket to identify remaining questions. Give brief oral feedback during presentations and written comments on submitted infographics.

lessonSections.heading: Sources informing the lesson
lessonSections.text: My revised plan draws on AERO’s “How Students Learn Best” for scaffolding and active engagement, Wiggins’ emphasis on transfer for the practical design task, and Hedengren’s approach to feedback as discovery for questions about audience and clarity. The NIH Plain Language Checklist supports the language revision activity. These are the sources identified in my first-semester revision.
